claims.text: The onset of premelting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is governed by preferential copper segregation to particle surfaces.
Surface-segregated copper forms a copper-enriched, low-melting liquid-like layer.
The copper-rich surface layer triggers and propagates nanoparticle melting.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are solid, homogeneous, single-phase, and uniformly distributed in elemental composition at room temperature.
Heating FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles through the premelting regime causes copper atoms to segregate to the surface.
Differences in atomic size, bonding characteristics, and surface energy drive copper surface segregation upon heating.
Copper has a relatively lower melting point than the relevant alloy baseline.
Copper segregation lowers the local melting temperature at the nanoparticle surface.
Melting initiates at the particle surface and gradually propagates inward.
FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles have a lower effective melting point than the homogeneous bulk alloy.
A liquid-like, copper-enriched surface layer should appear below the bulk melting point.
The premelted surface layer should grow inward as temperature increases.
The transition should progress from a solid nanoparticle to a fully molten particle.
Surface-driven premelting should be most significant for nanoparticles with high surface-to-volume ratios.
Larger particles and bulk samples should exhibit less pronounced surface-driven premelting.
Particle-size distribution, heating rate, atmosphere, oxidation, and contamination are to be controlled during the heating experiment.
Failure to observe copper segregation or a distinct surface liquid-like layer before bulk melting would falsify the proposed mechanism.
Premelting that occurs uniformly throughout the particle without surface copper enrichment would falsify the proposed mechanism.
